lesson.title: The Size Ceiling Every Link Enforces: Understanding MTU
lesson.summary: Maximum transmission unit sets the largest packet a link can carry in one frame, and packets that exceed it must be fragmented, blocked, or resized before they can pass.
lesson.body:
Maximum transmission unit, or MTU, is the largest packet size, measured in bytes, that a given communication link can carry in a single frame without needing to break it into pieces. It is a property of the link itself, not of any particular packet, and different technologies enforce different limits based on how their hardware and framing work.

The most familiar number here is 1500 bytes, the standard MTU for Ethernet, which has become the de facto default across most wired and Wi-Fi local networks because so much equipment is built to interoperate with it. Some networks support larger jumbo frames, often up to 9000 bytes, typically inside data centers where every device on the path is known to support the larger size. Other technologies impose smaller limits: PPPoE connections, common on some DSL setups, reduce the usable MTU to 1492 bytes because of extra encapsulation overhead, and older dial-up style links could be smaller still.

When a packet is larger than the MTU of a link it needs to cross, something has to give. In IPv4, routers are allowed to fragment an oversized packet into multiple smaller pieces that each fit within the link's MTU, with the destination reassembling them later. IPv4 packets also carry a do not fragment flag that senders can set to disable this, in which case an oversized packet is dropped and the router sends back an ICMP message indicating fragmentation was needed, which is how a technique called Path MTU Discovery finds the smallest MTU along an entire path. IPv6 goes further and does not allow routers to fragment packets in transit at all, placing the entire responsibility on the sending host to discover the path's MTU in advance and size its packets accordingly.

Fragmentation arithmetic illustrates the overhead involved. Suppose a host needs to send a 3,000 byte IP packet, meaning a 20 byte IP header plus 2,980 bytes of data, across a link with an MTU of 1,500 bytes. Each fragment also needs its own 20 byte IP header, leaving 1,480 bytes of data per fragment. The first fragment carries 1,480 bytes of data, the second carries another 1,480 bytes, using up 2,960 bytes total, and a third small fragment is needed for the remaining 20 bytes of data plus its own 20 byte header, for a 40 byte fragment. One original packet becomes three packets on the wire, with extra header bytes and extra processing at both ends.

MTU size involves a real trade-off that connects to two delay components covered earlier. A larger MTU means fewer packets are needed to carry the same amount of data, which reduces total header overhead and reduces the number of separate processing delay events at every router along the path. But a larger packet also takes longer to transmit, since transmission delay scales directly with packet size, and if a large packet is lost, more data has to be retransmitted at once. A smaller MTU produces more packets, each with its own header overhead and its own small transmission and processing delay, but any individual loss costs less data. Network designers choose MTU values as a balance between these costs rather than simply maximizing or minimizing packet size.
